You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-10.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Adversarial training (AT) has established itself as a leading method for model robustness; however, its success is largely confined to balanced datasets. In real-world scenarios exhibiting long-tailed class distributions, AT faces a critical failure mode: it disproportionately degrades the performance of minority (tail) classes. While standard long-tailed recognition techniques (such as re-weighting or logit adjustment) address clean accuracy imbalances, simply combining them with AT fails to produce sufficient adversarial robustness for tail classes. There is a lack of understanding regarding why AT exacerbates tail vulnerability more severely than natural training, and current methods fail to effectively transfer robustness knowledge to these data-scarce regions.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that the poor tail robustness in long-tailed adversarial training stems from the model's bias towards head classes during the generation of and defense against adversarial perturbations. We posit that a model trained on a *balanced* subset of data—even if artificially constructed and smaller in size—will develop superior robust features for tail classes compared to a model trained on the full, imbalanced distribution. By treating this balanced model as a "Self-Teacher," we can effectively distill its specific robust knowledge into the main model, thereby correcting the decision boundaries for minority classes without sacrificing the benefits of the full dataset.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)
We propose a two-stage "Self-Distillation" framework designed to decouple the learning of tail robustness from the learning of the full distribution.

1.  **Balanced Self-Teacher Construction:**
    *   We will generate a balanced sub-dataset from the original long-tailed source. This involves creating a set where every class has an equal number of samples, achieved via up-sampling tail data and down-sampling head data.
    *   We will train a "Self-Teacher" model on this balanced sub-dataset using standard adversarial training (e.g., PGD). The objective here is not to maximize overall accuracy, but specifically to acquire a model with high robustness in tail classes, which this balanced view facilitates.

2.  **Adversarial Self-Distillation:**
    *   We will train the primary "Student" model on the original, full long-tailed dataset to leverage all available information.
    *   To prevent the Student from neglecting tail robustness, we will employ a knowledge distillation mechanism. The Student will be supervised by the Balanced Self-Teacher.
    *   The loss function will be a composite:
        *   **Primary Loss:** A standard long-tailed adversarial loss (e.g., combining adversarial examples with a balanced softmax approach) to handle general classification.
        *   **Distillation Loss:** A regularization term forcing the Student’s predictions on adversarial examples to align with the Self-Teacher’s predictions. This explicitly guides the Student to mimic the Teacher’s robust decision boundaries in the minority class regions.

## Expected Contribution
*   **Theoretical Insight:** We aim to provide an analysis demonstrating that adversarial training inherently causes more severe performance degradation in tail classes compared to natural training, linking data imbalance directly to robust error amplification.
*   **Methodological Advancement:** We expect to introduce a simple, model-agnostic framework that surpasses the performance of methods that merely mix AT with re-weighting strategies.
*   **Performance Impact:** Ideally, this approach will yield State-of-the-Art robust accuracy for tail classes while maintaining high performance on head classes, effectively bridging the robustness gap in imbalanced learning scenarios.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We designed and executed a series of experiments to evaluate a novel two-step adversarial training framework involving self-distillation from a balanced self-teacher. The primary goal was to address the performance degradation of tail classes in long-tailed adversarial training.

**Datasets and Configuration**
*   **CIFAR-10-LT:** Long-tailed version of CIFAR-10. Imbalance Ratio (IR) set primarily to 50. Tail evaluation focused on the last class.
*   **CIFAR-100-LT:** Long-tailed version of CIFAR-100. IR set primarily to 10 (also tested 50, 20, 5). Tail evaluation focused on the last 10 classes.
*   **Tiny-ImageNet-LT:** Long-tailed version of Tiny-ImageNet. IR set to 10. Tail evaluation focused on the last 20 classes (out of 200).
*   **Data Augmentation:** Random crop and random horizontal flip were applied. RandAugment (RA) and AutoAugment (AuA) were used only in specific ablation studies.

**Model Architectures**
*   **CIFAR-10/100-LT:** ResNet-18 (primary) and WideResNet-34-10 (secondary/appendix).
*   **Tiny-ImageNet-LT:** PreActResNet-18.

**Training Implementation Details**
*   **Balanced Self-Teacher Training:**
    *   We constructed a balanced sub-dataset ($D_B$) by resampling the original long-tailed dataset.
    *   Sampling parameter $\gamma$ was set to $IR/2$.
    *   Training duration: 30 epochs.
    *   Batch size: 32.
    *   Optimizer: SGD (Learning rate 0.1, Weight decay $5 \times 10^{-4}$).
    *   Adversarial Attack: 10-step PGD with epsilon boundary 8/255.
*   **Main Student Training (Self-Distillation):**
    *   Training duration: 100 epochs.
    *   Batch size: 128.
    *   Optimizer: SGD (Learning rate 0.1, Weight decay $5 \times 10^{-4}$).
    *   Distillation: Performed using the pre-trained balanced self-teacher.
*   **Adversarial Constraints:** Epsilon boundary of 8/255; 10-step PGD attack used during training.

**Evaluation Metrics**
*   **Clean:** Standard accuracy on clean test data.
*   **PGD:** Robust accuracy under a 20-step PGD attack (epsilon 8/255).
*   **AA:** AutoAttack accuracy.
*   **T-Clean:** Clean accuracy specifically for the defined tail classes.
*   **T-PGD:** Robust accuracy specifically for the defined tail classes (20-step PGD).
*   **Checkpoints:** Performance was recorded at both the "Best Checkpoint" (based on PGD-20 accuracy) and the "Last Checkpoint".

**Baselines Compared**
*   **Standard Adversarial Training:** PGD-AT, TRADES, MART, AWP.
*   **Long-Tailed Adversarial Training:** RoBal, REAT, AT-BSL.

## 3. Qualitative Observations

**Theoretical Analysis Observations**
*   **Observation 1:** Theoretical derivation indicates that adversarial training causes more severe performance degradation in tail classes compared to natural training in long-tailed distributions.
*   **Observation 2:** As the imbalance ratio (IR) increases, the decision boundary of adversarially trained models becomes more distorted compared to naturally trained models, increasing sensitivity to perturbations in minority classes.
*   **Observation 3:** Both natural and robust errors of the tail class increase monotonically with respect to the imbalance ratio.

**Empirical Observations from Figures**
*   **Observation 4:** In CIFAR-100-LT experiments, our method surpassed all baselines in terms of overall clean accuracy and AutoAttack accuracy.
*   **Observation 5:** A scatter plot analysis of Tail Clean Accuracy vs. Tail PGD Accuracy revealed that our method achieved the highest performance in both metrics simultaneously, showing a distinct gap (superiority) over RoBal, REAT, and AT-BSL.
*   **Observation 6:** Experiments on binary logistic regression (Gaussian mixture) confirmed that as IR increases from 1 to 5, test accuracy for the tail class drops significantly for both natural and adversarial training, but adversarial training yields consistently higher robust errors than natural training.
*   **Observation 7:** In CIFAR-10-LT experiments, while adversarial training generally improved overall robustness compared to natural training, the natural model actually exhibited better robust performance on tail classes than the adversarially trained model, confirming the "tail vulnerability" hypothesis.

**Teacher and Hyperparameter Observations**
*   **Observation 8 (Teacher Selection):** When comparing different teachers (RoBal, REAT, AT-BSL, and PGD-AT on Balanced Subset $D_B$), the student model distilled from the $D_B$ teacher achieved the highest tail robust accuracy and tail clean accuracy, despite the $D_B$ teacher itself having lower overall performance.
*   **Observation 9 (Alpha Sensitivity):** Increasing the self-distillation weight parameter $\alpha$ resulted in improved robustness (both overall and tail) but a slight decrease in clean accuracy.
*   **Observation 10 (Gamma Sensitivity):** Increasing the sampling rate $\gamma$ (using more samples for the balanced self-teacher) led to improvements in both clean accuracy and robustness, though the sensitivity was less pronounced than for $\alpha$.

**Class-wise Performance Observations**
*   **Observation 11:** When analyzing robustness across 10 class groups (from head to tail), our method demonstrated higher robustness across all groups compared to the baseline (RoBal).
*   **Observation 12:** The baseline (RoBal) showed strong performance on head classes (first group) but performance degraded severely on the last group (tail classes). Our method maintained better consistency and achieved the best performance in the tail group.

references.text:
## Problem Statement
Adversarial training (AT) has been established as an effective method for enhancing robustness against adversarial attacks. However, current methodologies largely presume balanced data distributions. In real-world scenarios, data often follows a long-tailed distribution where a few head classes dominate, and tail classes are scarce.

Our preliminary analysis suggests a critical failure mode at the intersection of these two domains: adversarial training on long-tailed datasets disproportionately degrades the performance of tail classes. While existing approaches attempt to mitigate this by combining traditional long-tailed learning techniques (such as Balanced Softmax) with adversarial training, they fail to achieve sufficient robustness for the minority classes. We postulate that this is because standard long-tailed objectives focus on re-balancing margins based on sample counts but do not account for the intrinsic vulnerability of tail classes to adversarial perturbations. Consequently, we face a technical gap: there is no effective framework that simultaneously secures overall robustness and prevents the severe degradation of tail-class accuracy under adversarial attack.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose a novel, two-stage "Self-Distillation" framework to bridge this gap. Our core hypothesis is that a model trained on a strictly balanced subset of the data (even if that subset is smaller) learns significantly more robust features for tail classes than a model trained on the full, imbalanced dataset.

We hypothesize that by treating this "Balanced Self-Teacher" as a source of truth, we can distill its superior tail-robustness into a student model trained on the full long-tailed dataset. By decoupling the acquisition of tail robustness (via the teacher) from the learning of head-class features (via the student), we aim to achieve a model that maintains high overall accuracy while significantly reducing the robust error on tail classes compared to current state-of-the-art long-tailed adversarial training methods.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

### 1. Theoretical Analysis Framework
Before implementing the architecture, we will mathematically formalize the vulnerability of tail classes. We will model the binary classification problem on a long-tailed dataset with an imbalance ratio $r \geq 1$. We assume a Gaussian mixture distribution where the class labels $y$ and inputs $\mathbf{x}$ are defined as:

$$
y = \left\{ \begin{array} { l l } { + 1 , } & { \mathrm { w . p } ~ \frac { r } { r + 1 } } \\ { - 1 , } & { \mathrm { w . p } ~ \frac { 1 } { r + 1 } } \end{array} \right. , \quad x _ { 1 } , \cdot \cdot \cdot , x _ { n } \overset { i . i . d } { \sim } \mathcal { N } ( \eta y , 1 )
$$

Here, $\eta > \epsilon$ is a constant determining the standard deviation, and $\epsilon$ is the perturbation boundary. We will derive the theoretical bounds for the standard error $\mathcal{R}_{std}$ and robust error $\mathcal{R}_{rob}$ for the optimal natural classifier $f_{nat}^*$ and robust classifier $f_{rob}^*$. Specifically, we intend to prove that:

$$
\mathcal { R } _ { r o b } ^ { - 1 } ( f _ { r o b } ^ { * } ) > \mathcal { R } _ { r o b } ^ { - 1 } ( f _ { n a t } ^ { * } )
$$

This derivation will theoretically confirm that adversarial training exacerbates the vulnerability of the tail class (class $-1$) compared to natural training, motivating our distillation approach.

### 2. Balanced Self-Teacher Construction
The first phase of our pipeline involves training a "Self-Teacher" model, denoted as $f_B$.

1.  **Dataset Construction:** Given a long-tailed dataset $D$ with class counts $n_1 < n_2 < \dots < n_C$, we will construct a balanced sub-dataset $D_B$. We will define a hyperparameter $\gamma > 1$ and enforce that each class in $D_B$ contains $\gamma \cdot n_1$ samples. This involves down-sampling head classes and up-sampling tail classes.
2.  **Adversarial Training:** We will train $f_B$ on $D_B$ using Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) adversarial training. The objective is to minimize the standard cross-entropy loss on adversarial examples generated from $D_B$.

### 3. Main Training with Self-Distillation
The second phase trains the student model $f$ on the original long-tailed dataset $D$, utilizing knowledge distilled from $f_B$.

**Loss Function Formulation:**
The student model will be trained using a composite loss function consisting of the Balanced Softmax Loss (BSL) and a Knowledge Distillation (KD) term.

First, we define the **Balanced Softmax Loss**, which adjusts logits based on label frequencies to handle the long-tail distribution:

$$
\mathcal { L } _ { B S L } ( f ( \boldsymbol { x } ^ { \prime } ) , \boldsymbol { y } ) = - \log \Big ( \frac { e ^ { z _ { y } ^ { \prime } + b _ { y } } } { \sum _ { i } e ^ { z _ { i } ^ { \prime } + b _ { i } } } \Big )
$$

Where:
*   $\mathbf{x}'$ is the adversarially perturbed input generated via PGD.
*   $z'_i = f(\mathbf{x}')_i$ is the $i$-th logit of the student model on the adversarial input.
*   $b_i = \tau \cdot \log(n_i)$ is the adjustment term derived from the number of examples $n_i$ in class $i$, scaled by hyperparameter $\tau$.

Second, we incorporate **Self-Distillation**. We will utilize the logits from the balanced teacher $f_B$ to guide the student. We define the distillation loss $\mathcal{L}_{KD}$ as the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the teacher's soft probabilities and the student's probabilities on the adversarial examples.

**Algorithm Design:**
The training procedure will follow this specific sequence:

1.  **Teacher Phase:** Initialize $f_B$. For $T_B$ epochs, update $f_B$ using PGD-AT on batches sampled from $D_B$.
2.  **Student Phase:** Initialize $f$. For $T$ epochs, iterate through the full dataset $D$.
    *   For each mini-batch $\{\mathbf{x}_i, y_i\}$, generate adversarial examples $\mathbf{x}'_i$ using PGD.
    *   Compute teacher logits: $z^B = f_B(\mathbf{x}_i)$ (or potentially on perturbed inputs).
    *   Compute student logits: $z = f(\mathbf{x}'_i)$.
    *   Update student parameters $\theta$ via gradient descent to minimize the total objective:
        $$ \mathcal{L}_{total} = \mathcal{L}_{BSL} + \alpha \mathcal{L}_{KD} $$
        where $\alpha$ is a weighting hyperparameter.

## Expected Contribution
We anticipate this research will contribute the following to the field of robust deep learning:

1.  **Theoretical Formalization:** A rigorous proof demonstrating that adversarial training inherently causes greater performance degradation in tail classes compared to natural training in long-tailed distributions.
2.  **Novel Framework:** The introduction of the "Balanced Self-Distillation" strategy, providing a method to transfer tail-robustness from a balanced subset to a full-scale model.
3.  **State-of-the-Art Robustness:** We expect this architecture to outperform existing baselines (such as RoBal, REAT, and naive AT) specifically in **tail-class robust accuracy** against PGD and AutoAttack, without compromising clean accuracy or head-class performance.

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
